transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um, well, what brings me in is... I just can't seem to shake this really heavy mix of fear and guilt lately. It's like I'm just tense all day long, waiting for something else to go wrong, and I keep blaming myself for not stopping what happened. 

It's exhausting. I mean, I guess I'm used to looking for problems because I'm a building inspector, so my whole day is literally finding things that are wrong. You wouldn't believe the stuff contractors try to hide. Just Tuesday, this guy tried to pass off a completely unpermitted electrical panel in a commercial build, and I had to red-tag the whole site. He was furious, screaming about his deadlines. People always want to cut corners with cheap materials to save a buck, just like my uncle used to do when he'd fix up cars back home. He had this old Chevy truck that was practically held together with duct tape and prayers, and it broke down on us on the highway once when I was like ten... 

But anyway, wait, what was I saying? Oh, right. Sorry. Just... I'm just tired of feeling so guilty and on edge about everything.
Do you find yourself repeatedly thinking about the same things over and over, even when you try to stop?

Yeah, I do. It's... it's like a movie I can't turn off. Like, I'll be at work, right? Just measuring a railing or checking some drywall, or I'll hear a ladder scrape against the concrete, and out of nowhere, I just see it. I can see my husband falling, like it's happening right in front of me all over again. My stomach completely drops, and my hands get so shaky I can barely hold my clipboard. 

Which is a real problem, because if I drop my clipboard on a site, half the time it lands in mud or wet cement. You wouldn't believe how messy these sites get, especially after a good rain. The drainage on the new subdivision over on 4th Street is an absolute joke. I told the site manager last week, I said, "You're going to have a moat around these foundations if you don't grade this properly," but they just look at me like I'm crazy. It's just like when my cousin tried to landscape his own backyard and ended up flooding his basement because he didn't understand how a French drain works... 

But yeah, the thoughts just pop into my head like that, and I can't stop them.
Do these thoughts feel like they're forced into your mind, or are they more like thoughts you're intentionally thinking about?

No, no, I definitely don't try to think about it. Like I was just saying, they're completely forced. I'll just be standing there measuring a railing, minding my own business, or I'll hear that ladder scrape, and bam—out of nowhere, the memory is just forced into my head. I'm watching my husband fall all over again. My stomach drops, I get the shakes... I would never choose to feel that way. It's just so sudden. 

Honestly, it's as sudden as those pop-up thunderstorms we've been getting around here lately. You know, you'll be looking at a clear blue sky, and ten minutes later it's a torrential downpour. It completely ruins the framing on these new builds if they aren't wrapped right. I had to yell at a crew just yesterday because they left all this untreated lumber out in the rain, and lumber prices are way too high right now to just let it warp. My dad used to be a carpenter, and he would have lost his absolute mind if he saw how these kids treat wood today. He used to spend hours just sanding a single cabinet door until it was like glass. He built this beautiful oak dining table for my mom for their anniversary one year, and... 

Wait, sorry. What were we talking about? Oh, right. Yeah, the thoughts. They just force their way in. I don't want them there at all.
How long have you been experiencing these feelings of fear, guilt, and tension since your husband's fall?

Well, it's been about four months now. Yeah, four months since he fell while we were repairing the porch. 

Which, by the way, I told him we should have hired a professional for. I mean, I inspect buildings, I don't build them, and I definitely don't do structural repairs on century-old wraparound porches. Those things are a nightmare. You never know what kind of rot you're going to find under the floorboards until you pull them up. We had this house I inspected last month in the historic district, gorgeous Queen Anne style, but the entire foundation under the porch was basically powder from termite damage. The buyers were absolutely crushed when I told them they'd have to sink at least twenty grand into just stabilizing it before they could even think about painting. People get so attached to the aesthetics of a house they don't think about the bones. It's like buying a car just because you like the color, which is exactly what my sister did when she bought that lemon of a sedan right out of high school... 

But, um, yeah. Four months of this. Ever since the porch.
Do you find yourself avoiding certain places, activities, or conversations because they remind you of your husband's fall?

Yeah, I do. I mean, at work, I've started turning down jobs if they have raised porches or second-story decks. I just... I can't do it. And at home, I find excuses not to talk about the repair or even look at the spot where it happened. 

Which is actually really annoying because we still haven't finished the porch. It's just sitting there, half done, looking terrible. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she's always giving me these looks when she walks her dog past our house. She's got this little poodle mix, incredibly yappy thing, always barking at the mailman. I swear, that dog barks more than any dog I've ever met, and I see a lot of dogs on job sites. Some of the contractors bring their dogs to work, which I think is a huge liability. You know, you've got power tools and heavy machinery, and a dog running around? It's an accident waiting to happen. Just last week, this guy had his golden retriever on a site, and the dog almost knocked over a stack of drywall. Do you know how heavy drywall is? If that falls on you, it's not a joke. I had to write them up for safety violations, and the guy got so mad at me, but I'm just doing my job, you know? 

But anyway, yeah, I just avoid anything to do with porches or talking about the fall. I just stay away from it.
Has your guilt, fear, or these intrusive thoughts interfered with your relationships or daily activities outside of work?

Well, I mean... I'm still working. But it's definitely affecting things. Like I said, I've been turning down jobs with elevated decks or porches, which I used to handle without even thinking twice about it. And my inspection reports are taking way longer now because I just keep second-guessing myself. I'll read over a structural section three times just to make sure I didn't miss something. 

Which is frustrating because I used to be so fast at writing those up. I had this whole system down, a template I made myself in Excel. It had all the drop-down menus for common issues—like, you know, flashing problems around chimneys or improper grading near the foundation. Grading is actually a huge issue around here. People just pile mulch right up against their siding and wonder why they get water in their basement every spring. My uncle did that at his place. He had this beautiful split-level, but he insisted on doing his own landscaping. He put in these massive hostas right against the foundation, and of course, it completely messed up the drainage. The basement flooded, ruined his vintage record collection. He had original Beatles pressings down there, just sitting in cardboard boxes on the floor. Who puts valuable things on the floor in a basement? You'd think he'd at least put them on a pallet or a shelf. My mom was so mad at him because some of those records were actually hers from when they were teenagers...

Oh, but yeah. My reports are taking longer, and I'm avoiding the porch jobs. So, it's definitely getting in the way of things.
Are there things you used to enjoy doing in your free time that you've stopped doing because they remind you of your husband's fall or make you feel anxious?

I don't think so? I mean, my free time is pretty much the same as it was, except for the porch thing. I still watch my shows and go to my book club. We're reading this thriller right now, actually. It's about a woman who thinks her husband is a serial killer, but honestly, the author clearly did zero research on how police investigations actually work. They have the detective doing things that would get a case thrown out in two seconds. I was telling my friend Sarah about it—she's a paralegal—and she was just laughing at how absurd it was. Sarah reads a lot of non-fiction, mostly true crime, which I find a little too depressing, especially with everything going on in the world. You turn on the news and it's just one disaster after another. I used to watch the local news every morning while I had my coffee, but I had to stop because it was just ruining my mood before I even left the house. Now I just listen to this podcast about baking. I don't even bake! But the host has this really soothing voice, like one of those meditation apps... 

But no, I haven't really stopped doing anything I enjoy, other than just... not working on the house.
Do you find yourself avoiding conversations about your husband or the day of the accident with family and friends?

Yeah, I definitely do. Like I mentioned before, I just find excuses not to talk about it with anyone. If my family asks about the repair or how he's doing with everything, I just change the subject or say I have to go do something. I don't even want to look at the spot where it happened, let alone talk about that day. 

My sister tried to bring it up last week when we were at lunch. We went to this new bistro downtown, the one that took over the old hardware store space. Have you been there? The food is actually pretty good, but they kept the original hardwood floors, which look nice, but they echo so badly. It was so loud in there I could barely hear her. And they have these weird chairs that look like they're made of reclaimed barn wood, but they're incredibly uncomfortable. I don't understand this whole rustic-chic trend in restaurants. You're paying thirty dollars for a salad, you should at least get a cushion, right? And the waiter kept interrupting us right when she was trying to talk about it, which honestly, I was grateful for. He was this college kid, seemed really stressed out. I think they were short-staffed because there was a sign on the door saying they were hiring line cooks. It's so hard for places to keep staff right now. My friend who manages a coffee shop says people just don't show up for their shifts anymore... 

But yeah, I just avoid talking about it. Same with work, like I said, turning down the jobs with raised porches. I just steer clear of the whole topic.
Have you avoided any social activities because they remind you of your husband's fall?

Well, social activities? Not really. I mean, my friends don't usually hang out on raised porches or anything, so that's fine. It's really just the work thing, like I said, turning down those jobs with the second-story decks or elevated porches. And at home, I just find excuses not to talk about the repair or even look at that spot where it happened. 

Which is annoying because our backyard is usually really nice in the fall. We have this huge oak tree that turns this incredible shade of red. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he's always complaining about the leaves blowing into his yard, though. He's out there with his leaf blower at like 7 AM on a Saturday. Who does that? And it's gas-powered, so it smells awful and it's incredibly loud. I tried talking to him about maybe waiting until at least 9 AM, but he just grumbled something about having a schedule to keep. He's retired! What schedule? He spends half the day just standing in his driveway watching cars go by. He has this old Buick that he washes every single weekend, even if it hasn't rained. He uses this special chamois cloth and everything. My dad used to have a Buick, actually. It was this hideous shade of seafoam green, and the air conditioning never worked right. We drove it all the way to Florida one summer, and my brother and I were just sticking to the vinyl seats the whole way down. We stopped at this diner in Georgia where they served grits with every meal, even dinner, which I thought was so weird at the time... 

But yeah, socially I'm fine, I just don't want to look at the spot or do those specific jobs at work.
Do you ever feel like you're reliving the moment of your husband's fall, like you're right back there when it happened?

Yeah, I do. It's really awful. I'll be at work, just measuring a railing or something, or I'll hear a ladder scrape against the side of a house, and suddenly it's like I'm right back there. I can see him falling all over again, like it's happening right in front of me. My stomach just drops completely and my hands get all shaky. 

It actually happened the other day when I was inspecting this new build over in the West End. They're putting up all these townhouses over there, right where the old paper mill used to be. The developer is trying to market them as "luxury urban living," but honestly, the materials they're using are so cheap. I was looking at the drywall work in one of the units and it was a complete mess. The seams were practically visible from across the room. I don't know who they hired for the taping, but they clearly didn't care. And the paint colors they chose are so drab—just this endless sea of builder-grade beige. My cousin painted her whole house beige a few years ago because she read on some blog that it helps with resale value. But then she ended up staying there anyway, so now she just lives in a beige box. She has this tiny little pug named Waffles who perfectly blends into the carpet, so you have to shuffle your feet when you walk so you don't step on him. Waffles has a terrible underbite, so he always looks like he's judging you...

But yeah, the ladder scraping sound is the worst. It just brings it all back instantly and I get the shakes.
Do you ever feel like you're reliving the moment of your husband's fall, like you're right back there when it happened, and it feels as real as it did the first time?

Yeah, I think I just said that, didn't I? It's exactly like that. Like, I'll just be measuring a railing for work, or I'll hear that awful sound of a ladder scraping against siding, and boom—it's like I'm right back in that exact second. I see him falling all over again, plain as day, right in front of me. My stomach just totally drops out and my hands get all shaky. 

It's so hard to hide the shaking when you're holding a tape measure, you know? The metal part just rattles against whatever you're measuring. Tape measures are so flimsy these days anyway. I bought a new one from that big box store on the highway—the one that used to be a Sears before they all closed down. It's crazy how many empty storefronts there are in that plaza now. There's just the hardware store, a mattress place, and a pet supply store. I went into the pet store once to get a gift for my cousin's pug, Waffles—the one I was telling you about with the underbite? They had these little dog sweaters, but they were all made of this really scratchy acrylic yarn. I don't know why anyone would put that on a dog. I knit, actually, mostly scarves and hats, but I tried making a dog sweater once. It's surprisingly hard to get the armholes right. You have to measure the chest girth, which is nearly impossible with a squirmy dog... 

But yeah, the flashbacks or whatever you want to call them, they feel completely real. The ladder scraping sound is definitely the biggest trigger for it.
How often do these flashbacks of your husband's fall happen to you?

Well, it depends, I guess. It's not like an everyday thing, but it happens enough to be really bothersome. Like I mentioned, if I'm measuring a railing or if I hear that specific sound of a ladder scraping, out of nowhere I just see him falling all over again, right there in front of me. And my stomach drops, my hands get all shaky... 

It's really embarrassing when it happens at work, especially in front of the contractors. There's this one guy, Dave, who does a lot of the framing for the new subdivisions. He's always wearing these neon yellow safety shirts, even when he's just going to the deli for lunch. I saw him at the sandwich shop last Tuesday. They make this incredible turkey club there, with the really thick-cut bacon. But they always put way too much mayonnaise on it, even when you ask for just a little bit. I don't understand why sandwich places do that. It just makes the bread all soggy. My mom used to make the best sandwiches when we were kids. She'd use that really soft white bread that sticks to the roof of your mouth, and she'd cut the crusts off, not because we asked her to, but because she liked eating the crusts herself. She said it was the best part of the bread. She grew up during a time when they didn't waste anything, you know? She used to save bacon grease in this little ceramic jar on the stove... 

But anyway, yeah, the flashbacks happen whenever I'm around those triggers, like the railings or the ladders.
Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy doing?

No, I don't think so. I still like doing the things I usually do. Well, mostly knitting, like I mentioned before. I'm actually working on a scarf right now for my nephew. He's going off to college in upstate New York, and it gets freezing up there. I found this beautiful merino wool at this little yarn shop downtown. It's so much softer than that scratchy acrylic stuff they sell at the big craft stores. 

The woman who owns the yarn shop, Martha, is so sweet. She always has a pot of chamomile tea going and offers you a cup when you walk in. She has this huge gray cat named Barnaby who just sleeps in the front window all day. People actually stop on the sidewalk just to take pictures of him. I tried to pet him once, but he just gave me this look, kind of like Waffles the pug, you know? Just totally unimpressed. Martha says he used to be a stray, but you'd never know it now with how spoiled he is. She buys him this expensive grain-free salmon food that costs more than my own groceries. I was telling my sister about it, and she said... 

But no, I haven't really lost interest in my hobbies or anything like that. I still enjoy knitting just as much as I always have.
Have you avoided intimate relationships with your husband since the accident?

No, I don't... I mean, we're still close. We still, you know, have that part of our relationship. It hasn't really changed since the accident. He's actually been really great about everything, very patient. 

He's always been like that, though. Even when we first started dating, he was just so steady. We met at this terrible dive bar near the community college. It had those really sticky floors, you know the kind? Where your shoes make that peeling sound every time you take a step. They had this jukebox that only played '80s hair metal and country songs from the '90s. I think I played Shania Twain three times in a row just to annoy the bartender. The bartender was this guy named Rick who always wore these Hawaiian shirts, even in the dead of winter. He made the worst margaritas—just straight sour mix and cheap tequila. But they were only three dollars on Thursdays, so everyone went. That's where they put the new luxury apartments now, actually. They tore down the whole block last year. The construction took forever because they kept finding old pipes that weren't on the city plans. I had to go out there twice to inspect the foundation work, and the site manager was so stressed out he was practically pulling his hair out. He drank like four Red Bulls while I was there...

But yeah, to answer your question, no, I haven't been avoiding him or anything like that. We're fine in that department.
Have you avoided any other activities or places besides those related to your work or the porch where your husband fell?

Well, I guess I have been avoiding a few things. Like, with work, I've started turning down jobs if they involve raised porches or second-story decks. I just can't do it right now. And at home, I find all these excuses not to talk about fixing the porch, and I really try not to even look at the spot where he fell. 

It's actually really hard to avoid looking out back because our kitchen window faces right out to the yard. We have this beautiful oak tree back there. It drops acorns everywhere in the fall, which is a nightmare when you're trying to mow the lawn. You hear them shooting out from under the mower blades like little bullets. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, actually broke a window on his greenhouse last year because his lawnmower shot a rock right through the glass. He was so mad. He grows these amazing heirloom tomatoes in there, though. The really ugly, bumpy ones that taste incredible? He always brings us a basket of them in August. His wife used to make this fresh salsa with them, but she passed away a few years ago, so now he just eats them sliced with salt and pepper. He told me the secret to good tomatoes is putting crushed eggshells in the soil. I tried it with my basil plant, but I think I just ended up attracting raccoons to the patio...

But yeah, I definitely avoid anything with high decks at work, and I just try to stay away from the porch at home.
Have you avoided any social gatherings or events because they might remind you of the accident or make you feel anxious?

No, I haven't really avoided any social stuff because of it. I mean, we still go over to my sister's house for dinner most Sundays. She always makes this massive pot roast with potatoes and carrots. It's the same recipe our mom used to make, but my sister adds this splash of red wine to the gravy that just makes it so rich. She uses this really cheap cabernet, but you'd never know once it cooks down. 

Her husband always tries to get us to play these complicated board games after dinner. He buys them online, and they have like a million little pieces and rules that take an hour to explain. The last one we played was about building medieval cities, and I swear I spent half the time just trying to figure out what the little wooden sheep were for. They have a golden retriever who kept trying to eat the pieces off the coffee table. He's such a goofy dog, always carrying around this stuffed hedgehog toy that squeaks. It's missing one eye because the dog chewed it off the first day they got it... 

But no, I haven't been avoiding any social things. I'm still fine going out and seeing people.
Have you avoided other activities or places besides work and the porch that remind you of your husband's fall?

Um, no, not really. I mean, besides the porch and those high decks at work, I don't think there's anything else I'm staying away from. I still go to all my other inspection sites and everything. I drive my usual routes. 

Though, my work truck has been making this awful rattling noise lately. It's a Ford F-150, a few years old, and every time I hit about 45 miles an hour, it sounds like there's a tin can bouncing around under the passenger seat. I took it to this mechanic, Sal, over on 4th Street. My dad used to go to him all the time when I was a kid. Sal's shop always smells exactly the same—like burnt coffee and motor oil—and he still has this giant calendar on the wall with pictures of vintage muscle cars. He told me it was just a loose heat shield and fixed it for like twenty bucks. But while I was sitting in his waiting room, they had this daytime soap opera playing on the tiny TV in the corner, and the volume was so loud I couldn't even hear myself think. It was one of those shows where everyone is secretly related to everyone else, and this woman was crying because her twin sister stole her husband or something... 

Anyway, what were we saying? Oh, right, avoiding things. No, just the porch and the high stuff at work, really. That's about it.

Which is actually really annoying because we still haven't finished the porch. It's just sitting there, half done, looking terrible. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, she's always giving me these looks when she walks her dog past our house. She's got this little poodle mix, incredibly yappy thing, always barking at the mailman. I swear, that dog barks more than any dog I've ever met, and I see a lot of dogs on job sites. Some of the contractors bring their dogs to work, which I think is a huge liability. You know, you've got power tools and heavy machinery, and a dog running around? It's an accident waiting to happen. Just last week, this guy had his golden retriever on a site, and the dog almost knocked over a stack of drywall. Do you know how heavy drywall is? If that falls on you, it's not a joke. I had to write them up for safety violations, and the guy got so mad at me, but I'm just doing my job, you know? 

But anyway, yeah, I just avoid anything to do with porches or talking about the fall. I just stay away from it.

patient.answer:
Well, I mean... I'm still working. But it's definitely affecting things. Like I said, I've been turning down jobs with elevated decks or porches, which I used to handle without even thinking twice about it. And my inspection reports are taking way longer now because I just keep second-guessing myself. I'll read over a structural section three times just to make sure I didn't miss something. 

Which is frustrating because I used to be so fast at writing those up. I had this whole system down, a template I made myself in Excel. It had all the drop-down menus for common issues—like, you know, flashing problems around chimneys or improper grading near the foundation. Grading is actually a huge issue around here. People just pile mulch right up against their siding and wonder why they get water in their basement every spring. My uncle did that at his place. He had this beautiful split-level, but he insisted on doing his own landscaping. He put in these massive hostas right against the foundation, and of course, it completely messed up the drainage. The basement flooded, ruined his vintage record collection. He had original Beatles pressings down there, just sitting in cardboard boxes on the floor. Who puts valuable things on the floor in a basement? You'd think he'd at least put them on a pallet or a shelf. My mom was so mad at him because some of those records were actually hers from when they were teenagers...

Oh, but yeah. My reports are taking longer, and I'm avoiding the porch jobs. So, it's definitely getting in the way of things.

I don't think so? I mean, my free time is pretty much the same as it was, except for the porch thing. I still watch my shows and go to my book club. We're reading this thriller right now, actually. They have the detective doing things that would get a case thrown out in two seconds. I was telling my friend Sarah about it—she's a paralegal—and she was just laughing at how absurd it was. Sarah reads a lot of non-fiction, mostly true crime, which I find a little too depressing, especially with everything going on in the world. You turn on the news and it's just one disaster after another. I used to watch the local news every morning while I had my coffee, but I had to stop because it was just ruining my mood before I even left the house. Now I just listen to this podcast about baking. I don't even bake! But the host has this really soothing voice, like one of those meditation apps... 

But no, I haven't really stopped doing anything I enjoy, other than just... not working on the house.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I definitely do. Like I mentioned before, I just find excuses not to talk about it with anyone. If my family asks about the repair or how he's doing with everything, I just change the subject or say I have to go do something. I don't even want to look at the spot where it happened, let alone talk about that day. 

My sister tried to bring it up last week when we were at lunch. We went to this new bistro downtown, the one that took over the old hardware store space. Have you been there? The food is actually pretty good, but they kept the original hardwood floors, which look nice, but they echo so badly. It was so loud in there I could barely hear her. And they have these weird chairs that look like they're made of reclaimed barn wood, but they're incredibly uncomfortable. I don't understand this whole rustic-chic trend in restaurants. You're paying thirty dollars for a salad, you should at least get a cushion, right? And the waiter kept interrupting us right when she was trying to talk about it, which honestly, I was grateful for. He was this college kid, seemed really stressed out. I think they were short-staffed because there was a sign on the door saying they were hiring line cooks. It's so hard for places to keep staff right now. My friend who manages a coffee shop says people just don't show up for their shifts anymore... 

But yeah, I just avoid talking about it. Same with work, like I said, turning down the jobs with raised porches. I just steer clear of the whole topic.

Well, social activities? Not really. I mean, my friends don't usually hang out on raised porches or anything, so that's fine. It's really just the work thing, like I said, turning down those jobs with the second-story decks or elevated porches. And at home, I just find excuses not to talk about the repair or even look at that spot where it happened. 

Which is annoying because our backyard is usually really nice in the fall. We have this huge oak tree that turns this incredible shade of red. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he's always complaining about the leaves blowing into his yard, though. He's out there with his leaf blower at like 7 AM on a Saturday. Who does that? And it's gas-powered, so it smells awful and it's incredibly loud. I tried talking to him about maybe waiting until at least 9 AM, but he just grumbled something about having a schedule to keep. He's retired! What schedule? He spends half the day just standing in his driveway watching cars go by. He has this old Buick that he washes every single weekend, even if it hasn't rained. He uses this special chamois cloth and everything. My dad used to have a Buick, actually. It was this hideous shade of seafoam green, and the air conditioning never worked right. We drove it all the way to Florida one summer, and my brother and I were just sticking to the vinyl seats the whole way down. We stopped at this diner in Georgia where they served grits with every meal, even dinner, which I thought was so weird at the time... 

But yeah, socially I'm fine, I just don't want to look at the spot or do those specific jobs at work.

doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you're reliving the moment of your husband's fall, like you're right back there when it happened?

target_item.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I'll be measuring a railing or just hearing a ladder scrape, and out of nowhere I can see my husband falling like it's happening right in front of me, with my stomach dropping and my hands getting shaky.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I ever feel like I am reliving the traumatic event (flashbacks/intrusive memories), which directly corresponds to the Intrusive Symptoms profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I do. It's really awful. I'll be at work, just measuring a railing or something, or I'll hear a ladder scrape against the side of a house, and suddenly it's like I'm right back there. I can see him falling all over again, like it's happening right in front of me. My stomach just drops completely and my hands get all shaky. 

It actually happened the other day when I was inspecting this new build over in the West End. They're putting up all these townhouses over there, right where the old paper mill used to be. The developer is trying to market them as "luxury urban living," but honestly, the materials they're using are so cheap. I was looking at the drywall work in one of the units and it was a complete mess. The seams were practically visible from across the room. I don't know who they hired for the taping, but they clearly didn't care. And the paint colors they chose are so drab—just this endless sea of builder-grade beige. My cousin painted her whole house beige a few years ago because she read on some blog that it helps with resale value. But then she ended up staying there anyway, so now she just lives in a beige box. She has this tiny little pug named Waffles who perfectly blends into the carpet, so you have to shuffle your feet when you walk so you don't step on him. Waffles has a terrible underbite, so he always looks like he's judging you...

But yeah, the ladder scraping sound is the worst. It just brings it all back instantly and I get the shakes.

doctor.question: Do you ever feel like you're reliving the moment of your husband's fall, like you're right back there when it happened, and it feels as real as it did the first time?

target_item.name: Intrusive_Symptoms
target_item.manifestation: I'll be measuring a railing or just hearing a ladder scrape, and out of nowhere I can see my husband falling like it's happening right in front of me, with my stomach dropping and my hands getting shaky.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about flashbacks and reliving the traumatic event, which directly maps to intrusive symptoms.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think I just said that, didn't I? It's exactly like that. Like, I'll just be measuring a railing for work, or I'll hear that awful sound of a ladder scraping against siding, and boom—it's like I'm right back in that exact second. I see him falling all over again, plain as day, right in front of me. My stomach just totally drops out and my hands get all shaky. 

It's so hard to hide the shaking when you're holding a tape measure, you know? The metal part just rattles against whatever you're measuring. Tape measures are so flimsy these days anyway. I bought a new one from that big box store on the highway—the one that used to be a Sears before they all closed down. It's crazy how many empty storefronts there are in that plaza now. There's just the hardware store, a mattress place, and a pet supply store. I went into the pet store once to get a gift for my cousin's pug, Waffles—the one I was telling you about with the underbite? They had these little dog sweaters, but they were all made of this really scratchy acrylic yarn. I don't know why anyone would put that on a dog. I knit, actually, mostly scarves and hats, but I tried making a dog sweater once. It's surprisingly hard to get the armholes right. You have to measure the chest girth, which is nearly impossible with a squirmy dog... 

But yeah, the flashbacks or whatever you want to call them, they feel completely real. The ladder scraping sound is definitely the biggest trigger for it.

Well, it depends, I guess. It's not like an everyday thing, but it happens enough to be really bothersome. And my stomach drops, my hands get all shaky... 

It's really embarrassing when it happens at work, especially in front of the contractors. There's this one guy, Dave, who does a lot of the framing for the new subdivisions. He's always wearing these neon yellow safety shirts, even when he's just going to the deli for lunch. I saw him at the sandwich shop last Tuesday. They make this incredible turkey club there, with the really thick-cut bacon. But they always put way too much mayonnaise on it, even when you ask for just a little bit. I don't understand why sandwich places do that. It just makes the bread all soggy. My mom used to make the best sandwiches when we were kids. She'd use that really soft white bread that sticks to the roof of your mouth, and she'd cut the crusts off, not because we asked her to, but because she liked eating the crusts herself. She said it was the best part of the bread. She grew up during a time when they didn't waste anything, you know? She used to save bacon grease in this little ceramic jar on the stove... 

But anyway, yeah, the flashbacks happen whenever I'm around those triggers, like the railings or the ladders.

She has this huge gray cat named Barnaby who just sleeps in the front window all day. People actually stop on the sidewalk just to take pictures of him. I tried to pet him once, but he just gave me this look, kind of like Waffles the pug, you know? Just totally unimpressed. Martha says he used to be a stray, but you'd never know it now with how spoiled he is. She buys him this expensive grain-free salmon food that costs more than my own groceries. I was telling my sister about it, and she said...

It had those really sticky floors, you know the kind? Where your shoes make that peeling sound every time you take a step. They had this jukebox that only played '80s hair metal and country songs from the '90s. I think I played Shania Twain three times in a row just to annoy the bartender. The bartender was this guy named Rick who always wore these Hawaiian shirts, even in the dead of winter. He made the worst margaritas—just straight sour mix and cheap tequila. But they were only three dollars on Thursdays, so everyone went. That's where they put the new luxury apartments now, actually. They tore down the whole block last year. The construction took forever because they kept finding old pipes that weren't on the city plans. I had to go out there twice to inspect the foundation work, and the site manager was so stressed out he was practically pulling his hair out. He drank like four Red Bulls while I was there...
